paper_metadata.title: Quantum computational finance: Monte Carlo pricing of financial derivatives

summary: The paper presents a quantum Monte Carlo pricing framework for financial derivatives, showing an asymptotic improvement from O(1/epsilon^2) classical sampling to O(1/epsilon) quantum amplitude estimation for European call options, with bounded-variance complexity ~O(lambda/epsilon). It also extends the construction to arithmetic Asian options using L discretized Brownian increments, but reports no hardware experiment or concrete qubit/gate counts for either case.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo pricing of a European call option using amplitude estimation / phase estimation on a discretized Brownian motion distribution and payoff circuit.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo pricing with amplitude estimation and phase estimation

hyperparameters.discretization_qubits: n qubits for Brownian motion discretization
hyperparameters.phase_estimation_register: m-qubit register in theory; single-qubit phase-estimation surrogate in numerics
hyperparameters.success_probability_theorem: at least 8/pi^2 for basic amplitude estimation, boosted to 1-delta by median trick

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Prepare discretized Gaussian Brownian-motion state G|0^n> = sum_j sqrt(p_j)|j>; encode payoff via controlled rotation on ancilla using discretized payoff values v(x_j).
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate option price Pi = e^{-rT} E_Q[f(S_T)] = e^{-rT} E_Q[v(W_T)] for European call payoff f(S_T)=max(0,S_T-K).

problem_instance.description: European call option under Black-Scholes-Merton model.

dataset_specification.description: Parameters used in numerics: S0=$100, K=$50, r=0.05, sigma=0.2, T=1; analytical price used as benchmark.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize Brownian motion on [-x_max, x_max] with 2^n points; approximate payoff with n-bit binary function; use Gaussian probability density p_T(x).
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Classical numerical simulations comparing quantum phase-estimation error scaling against classical Monte Carlo; confidence >99.5%; fit error to power law over number of Monte Carlo steps.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Analytical Black-Scholes price used to set phase theta in single-qubit phase-estimation numerics; discretize Gaussian distribution and payoff.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Estimate option price from measured phase / ancilla probability; discount by e^{-rT}.

speedup_claims.conditions: for additive error epsilon; classical sampling scales as O(1/epsilon^2) while quantum amplitude estimation scales as O(1/epsilon) up to polylog factors
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper’s numerical section uses a single-qubit phase-estimation surrogate rather than a full fault-tolerant implementation; the quadratic scaling is supported by theory and numerical fits.

speedup_claims.conditions: European call option numerics with S0=100, K=50, r=0.05, sigma=0.2, T=1, D≈24, over the plotted Monte Carlo-step range
speedup_claims.caveats: This is inferred from fitted exponents ζQ=-0.982 and ζC=-0.5, not a direct runtime speedup.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(1/epsilon) applications of U for additive error epsilon (up to polylog factors); total ˜O(lambda/epsilon) in the bounded-variance setting
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(1/epsilon^2) samples for Monte Carlo estimation

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not reported; only asymptotic O(1/epsilon) vs O(1/epsilon^2) scaling and a toy single-qubit phase-estimation surrogate are shown
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Efficient state preparation of the discretized Gaussian distribution and reversible payoff circuit; no concrete qubit count, depth, or gate counts are reported for a full device implementation
limiting_factors: Only classical numerical simulations are reported
Quadratic speedup is asymptotic and likely overwhelmed by fault-tolerance overhead
State preparation and reversible arithmetic are nontrivial

notes: Hardware is not a real QPU experiment; the paper states numerics were performed with a single-qubit phase-estimation surrogate and mentions Strawberry Fields / ProjectQ for simulation, so hardware.type is inferred as simulator_other.
The paper does not report a concrete qubit count for the full algorithmic experiment; n and m are symbolic, so num_qubits is null/inferred only at the symbolic level.
No transpiled depth, gate counts, or shot counts are reported.
The paper claims a quadratic speedup in sample complexity, but the evidence is theoretical and based on simulations/analysis rather than a hardware demonstration.

experiments.description: Quantum Monte Carlo pricing of an arithmetic Asian call option using product-state preparation of multiple Brownian increments and amplitude estimation.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo pricing of Asian options with amplitude estimation

hyperparameters.distribution_preparation: Grover-Rudolph state preparation for each increment
hyperparameters.success_probability_theorem: at least 2/3 for bounded-variance mean estimation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Prepare L copies of discretized Gaussian increment states |p_Delta t>; compute path-dependent arithmetic or geometric average in a reversible circuit; encode payoff via ancilla rotation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate Asian call price with payoff f(A_T)=max(0,A_T-K), where A_T is arithmetic or geometric mean of sampled stock prices along the path.

problem_instance.description: Asian option pricing in the Black-Scholes-Merton model; arithmetic Asian option emphasized as requiring Monte Carlo.

dataset_specification.description: Equally spaced time points t_l with Delta t = T/L; stock path generated from Brownian increments.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize each Brownian increment with m qubits; prepare product state of L increment distributions; compute running arithmetic/geometric mean sequentially.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: The paper provides algorithmic resource discussion and theoretical speedup; no separate numerical Asian-option benchmark is reported.

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Prepare L Gaussian increment states; compute stock path recursively via S_{t_{l+1}} = S_{t_l} exp(sigma x + (r-sigma^2/2)Delta t).
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Estimate option price from ancilla success probability and discounting.

speedup_claims.conditions: bounded-variance mean estimation for Asian option pricing; classical scaling O(1/epsilon^2) versus quantum O((lambda/epsilon) polylog(lambda/epsilon))
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper gives an algorithmic extension and resource scaling, but no separate numerical Asian-option benchmark is reported.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O((lambda/epsilon) polylog(lambda/epsilon)) applications of U in the bounded-variance setting
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(1/epsilon^2) samples for Monte Carlo estimation

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: L copies of discretized Brownian increment states, reversible path averaging, and ancilla rotation; no concrete resource estimate for a specific instance
limiting_factors: No numerical Asian-option benchmark is reported
Resource scaling is symbolic in L and m only
Data loading and path-state preparation dominate

notes: This is a theoretical algorithmic extension; no hardware run is reported, so hardware.type is not_specified/inferred from context.
The paper gives symbolic resource scaling in terms of L and m but no concrete qubit count, depth, or gate counts for a specific Asian-option instance.
The Asian-option section is an algorithmic extension with theoretical scaling only.
